title: Stanford violated its AI policy by turning a Hispanic student into a fake Black woman in ad

reading.body:
This is a case of an institution using a generative editing tool to change the identity of a real, identifiable person in its own promotional material, then publishing the result without disclosure. The failure sits at the point of production and review, not in the model itself: the image was altered, and no step between alteration and display caught it. Catching it would have required a check that compared the published banner against the source photograph and against the university's own stated rule, which already prohibited exactly this use.

The failure mode is an impersonation of a specific person, combined with a system used outside the conditions it was built for. The tool produced a fabricated depiction of an individual who did not consent to it, and the institution presented that fabrication as a photograph of its students. The university itself characterised both the alteration and the absence of disclosure as violations of its policy, so the gap between the rule and the practice is documented rather than alleged.

What is not established is intent. The reports describe the alteration and the policy breach, and the university has acknowledged both, but nothing in the facts given shows who made the edit, why the substitution was made, or whether anyone understood at the time that a real student was being replaced.

reports.title: Stanford Used A.I. to Swap Black Student for Hispanic Student in a Photo
Stanford R&DE Uses AI to Race Swap Students for Advertising
University confirms use of AI-edited photo amid controversy
Stanford violated its AI policy by turning a Hispanic student into a fake Black woman in ad

summary:
Stanford University used artificial intelligence to alter a photo of students for banners on campus. Billy Ramirez, a Hispanic senior majoring in human biology, appeared in the original 2024 photo taken at a Lunar New Year party. In the banner version, he was replaced by a Black woman, and two other students were made to look thinner. Ramirez learned about the change from a friend and said he felt erased and upset.

Stanford acknowledged the alteration and said its policy strictly prohibits using A.I. to change images of Stanford people, events, research, facilities or achievements. The university said both the alteration and the lack of disclosure violated that policy. Stanford is working with Residential and Dining Enterprises to provide additional training and ensure proper review of all materials.
